title: Утиная охота на Джекил-Айленде
distraction: Публика видела «реформу против банкиров». Проект системы писали сами банкиры, тайно.
facts: В ноябре 1910 года сенатор Нелсон Олдрич и пятеро финансистов и чиновников (Пол Варбург, Фрэнк Вандерлип, Генри Дэвисон, Бенджамин Стронг, А. Пиатт Эндрю) уехали в частный клуб на острове Джекил-Айленд в Джорджии.
Поездку замаскировали под утиную охоту. Участники ехали в частном вагоне и, по воспоминаниям, обращались друг к другу только по именам, чтобы не привлекать внимания.
Там написали «план Олдрича», который стал основой Закона о Федеральной резервной системе, подписанного 23 декабря 1913 года.
Вандерлип сам описал встречу в 1935 году. Сегодня её историю публикует сам ФРС на сайте Federal Reserve History.
sources: Federal Reserve History: «The Jekyll Island Conference»
Frank Vanderlip, From Farm Boy to Financier (1935)

vo.text: In 1910, six men went on a duck hunt. They didn't shoot a single duck.
A senator. Bankers from the biggest houses on Wall Street. A private train car. First names only.
Destination: a private island club in Georgia.
What they wrote there became the blueprint for the Federal Reserve. Signed into law three years later.
This isn't a theory. The Fed tells this story on its own website.
The lesson? The rules of money were never written by the people who use it. So learn them.

en.title: The Duck Hunt on Jekyll Island
en.distraction: The public saw a “reform against the bankers.” The blueprint for the system was written by the bankers themselves, in secret.
facts: In November 1910, Senator Nelson Aldrich and five financiers and officials (Paul Warburg, Frank Vanderlip, Henry Davison, Benjamin Strong, A. Piatt Andrew) went to a private club on Jekyll Island, Georgia.
The trip was disguised as a duck hunt. The participants traveled in a private railcar and, according to recollections, addressed each other by first names only to avoid attracting attention.
There they wrote the “Aldrich Plan,” which became the basis of the Federal Reserve Act, signed on December 23, 1913.
Vanderlip himself described the meeting in 1935. Today the Fed itself publishes its story on the Federal Reserve History website.
sources: Federal Reserve History: “The Jekyll Island Conference”
Frank Vanderlip, From Farm Boy to Financier (1935)
risks: Don't claim the Fed is “owned” by particular families: that's a popular myth.
Stick to documented facts: the meeting, the participants, the cover story, the Aldrich Plan, the 1913 Act.

expert.markets: The backstory is the Panic of 1907, when J.P. Morgan effectively rescued the banking system. That created the demand for a “lender of last resort.”
expert.macro: Today it's the Fed that sets the rate and manages liquidity. Knowing its origins explains why markets react to every FOMC meeting.
expert.politics: The secrecy was because in 1910 the public distrusted Wall Street: a plan coming from bankers would have failed immediately. It shows how framing shapes the perception of a reform.

Except they didn't steal a safe — they took the right to write the rules of money. Trailer-style humor, ending on an honest takeaway with no demonizing.
